items.title: The console
items.text: Production stopped by the end of March 2001. Remaining stock was sold at $99 in the United States, and Sega booked ¥11.1 billion of final hardware and accessory sales in fiscal 2002.[^5][^3]

items.title: Sega
items.text: In its first year without a console Sega sold 7.07 million games for other companies’ machines, 3.5 million of them on the PlayStation 2, and returned to operating profit.[^3] It is now part of Sega Sammy Holdings.[^25]

items.title: The 2K sports studio
items.text: Visual Concepts, bought for $10 million to replace EA’s sports games,[^7] went to Take-Two with the 2K brand for about $24 million in January 2005.[^26]

items.title: Peter Moore
items.text: He joined Microsoft in 2003 to work on Xbox and moved to Electronic Arts in 2007.[^8][^9]

items.title: Isao Okawa
items.text: The chairman who gave Sega his shares died on March 16, 2001. In April 2001 the sega.com home page carried the line “In memory Isao Okawa 1926–2001.”[^2][^27]

items.title: The idea
items.text: Moore said the Dreamcast “was the precursor to the next-gen consoles” because it went online first, even with SegaNet at “just 50,000 people.”[^6] Sega’s 2002 report says it “created the first online console gaming network with Dreamcast.”[^3]

blocks.title: Who has owned the Dreamcast name
blocks.subtitle: The brand never left Sega. The company around it changed.
